strengths.point: The deck is clear-eyed and honest about the financial constraint the client operates under.
strengths.quote: Client D has no cash reserves and cannot take on new fixed costs without new income first. The board has been clear that hiring is not possible until revenue grows.

findings.title: The recommendation to hire and sign a lease contradicts the deck's own stated constraint that no new fixed costs are possible until revenue grows.
findings.principle: Internal consistency: a recommendation must respect the constraints the deck itself establishes.
findings.diagnosis: Slide 3 states the client has no cash reserves, cannot take on new fixed costs without new income first, and that the board has ruled out hiring until revenue grows. Slide 6 then recommends opening a shopfront and hiring three paid staff now. The plan requires exactly the new fixed costs slide 3 says are impossible, so the recommendation walks into its own barrier.

evidence.quote: Client D has no cash reserves and cannot take on new fixed costs without new income first. The board has been clear that hiring is not possible until revenue grows.
Open a retail shopfront within six months and hire three paid repair staff to meet demand.

findings.why: A board that has said it cannot hire until revenue grows will reject a plan that opens with hiring and a lease, and the credibility of the whole deck falls with the contradiction.
findings.reflect: How does the client fund the lease and three salaries before the new revenue arrives, given slide 3 says it cannot.
findings.fix: Reconcile the recommendation with the constraint. Either sequence a low-fixed-cost revenue step first and add staff only once income supports it, or show explicitly how the gap is bridged and why the board's stated limit no longer binds.

findings.title: The financial case rests on doubling figures that carry no source, baseline or method.
findings.principle: Evidence Grounding: a number that drives the decision must be sourced.
findings.diagnosis: The recommendation depends on revenue doubling and the shop paying for itself, and on peers having doubled revenue. Slide 5 and slide 7 state these as facts with no source, no baseline and no method, so the financial case is unsupported.

evidence.quote: Revenue will double in year one. The shop pays for itself by month nine.
Comparable social enterprises have doubled revenue after opening a shop.

findings.why: A board deciding whether to commit scarce reserves to a lease needs to know where the doubling comes from, and an unsourced projection reads as invented.
findings.reflect: What evidence stands behind the doubling projection, and what would you accept as a credible basis for it.
findings.fix: Source the projection from the peer cases or a bottom-up model, show the baseline and assumptions, and present a range rather than a point figure. If it cannot be sourced, mark it as an assumption and test whether the recommendation survives without it.

findings.title: The deck calls the plan low-risk while its own facts show the client has no reserves and falling grants.
findings.principle: Honest uncertainty: certainty must match the evidence, and downside must be named.
findings.diagnosis: Slide 8 asserts the plan is low-risk, but slide 2 and slide 3 establish falling grant income and no cash reserves. A lease and three salaries committed against an unsourced revenue projection is a high-downside bet for an organization that cannot absorb a loss, so the low-risk label understates the real exposure.

evidence.quote: Client D has no cash reserves and cannot take on new fixed costs without new income first.

findings.why: Telling a board with no reserves that a fixed-cost commitment is low-risk invites a decision the client cannot recover from if revenue does not double.
findings.reflect: If revenue grows half as fast as projected, what happens to the lease and the three salaries, and can the client survive it.
findings.fix: State the load-bearing assumptions and the downside case, and name what happens if revenue undershoots. Replace the low-risk claim with an honest risk and mitigation.

findings.title: Slide titles are topic labels, so the argument is not readable from the titles alone.
findings.principle: Pyramid Principle: titles carry the message as complete-sentence assertions.
findings.diagnosis: Titles such as The opportunity and Why this works are labels, not assertions. A reader skimming the titles cannot reconstruct the recommendation or the reasoning behind it.
findings.why: A busy board member reading only the titles cannot follow the case, so the argument does not land on its own.
findings.reflect: If the client saw only your slide titles, could they state the recommendation and one reason for it.
findings.fix: Rewrite content titles as full-sentence assertions that state the takeaway of each slide, so the titles alone carry the argument.

comments.problem: Next steps name no owner and no date ("Sign a lease. Recruit staff. Launch.").
comments.why: Without an owner and a date no one is accountable and the sequence hides the constraint problem.
comments.fix: Give the first steps an owner and a date, and sequence them so revenue precedes fixed costs.

questionsForLead: Did the team reconcile the board's position that hiring is not possible until revenue grows with the recommendation to hire three staff now.
Where does the revenue-doubling projection come from, and did anyone verify the peer comparison.
Is there a phased or lower-fixed-cost option that respects the no-cash-reserves constraint on slide 3.

learningNote.lesson: A recommendation must survive a check against the constraints the deck itself establishes. If your own earlier slide rules something out, the recommendation cannot quietly assume it.
learningNote.weakHabit: Reaching for the ambitious solution and not testing it against the client's stated limits and evidence.
learningNote.exercise: List every constraint and every load-bearing number the deck states, then hold the final recommendation against each one and mark where it conflicts or depends on an unsourced figure.
